clinicalPearls: Addiction is established when nicotine in any form (combusted or heated tobacco, oral pouches, or vaped nicotine/nicotine salt) is used with sufficient intensity for a sufficient duration; addicted users self-titrate the frequency and intensity of use to achieve psychoactive effects and avoid withdrawal.

The diagnosis is clinical and hinges on loss of control over the next use of a nicotine product, evidenced by daily use, high number of episodes per day, use shortly after waking, craving during abstinence, and prior failed quit attempts.

The clinically important metric is the cumulative frequency of any nicotine dosing across all products used, not the specific product source, because it is dosing frequency that creates and sustains addiction.

Nicotine itself causes relatively little disease (notably pregnancy complications); the majority of disease burden comes from repetitive exposure to the carcinogens and toxicants carried with nicotine in various products, which addiction drives by compelling multiple daily exposures.
Withdrawal symptoms intensify with longer abstinence as blood nicotine falls and detaches from receptors, and these symptoms can persist for roughly 4-6 weeks.

Acidic aerosols (cigarettes and nicotine salt vaping devices) reduce airway irritation, permit deep inhalation, and produce rapid arterial nicotine rises reaching the brain, making them more addictive than products with slower delivery.
Cancer risk rises linearly with the number of cigarettes per day and logarithmically with duration of smoking; relative risk of lung cancer in current smokers ranges roughly 13-28 across age groups.

Cigarette smoking accounts for about 80% of COPD, about 90% of peripheral vascular disease in nondiabetics, about 50% of aortic aneurysms, about 24% of coronary artery disease, and about 11% of strokes.

Smoking induces the cytochrome P450 system, which can lower serum levels of drugs such as warfarin; conversely, levels may rise during hospitalization when a patient stops smoking, an important consideration for narrow-therapeutic-index agents.

About 40% of cigarette smokers die prematurely from smoking unless they quit; the population still smoking has shifted toward socially disadvantaged groups, and prevalence has declined more slowly in those over 40 who are most likely to develop disease.

'Lower tar/nicotine' filtered cigarettes do not reduce real exposure because smokers compensate by altering puffing behavior or number smoked; ventilation-hole designs lower only machine-measured yields, not delivered toxicants.

Several genes are associated with nicotine addiction (some reducing nicotine clearance, others increasing dependence likelihood or depression risk), but the large declines in smoking since the mid-1950s indicate non-genetic factors dominate population trends.
harrison.pathophysiology: Nicotine reaching the brain reversibly binds nicotinic acetylcholine receptors that are highly active in networks mediating mood, reward, joy, and excitement. With sustained high exposure, nicotinic receptors are upregulated on brain cells, so that for most people daily use is required to maintain the addicted state. As blood nicotine falls between doses, nicotine detaches from receptors and addicted individuals no longer feel 'normal,' producing a compulsive drive for the next dose. The strength and speed of addiction depend on dosing frequency and on the arterial nicotine concentration reaching the brain, which varies by product. Unprotonated (freebase) nicotine, favored at alkaline pH, is absorbed readily across mucosa but is airway-irritating at high concentration; addictive products use mildly acidic aerosols in the mouth to limit irritation and permit deep inhalation, after which alveolar pH shifts toward blood pH (~7.4), rapidly liberating absorbable unprotonated nicotine and driving fast arterial rises to the brain.
additionalDifferentials: Other substance use disorders (alcohol use disorder, stimulant use)
Primary mood or anxiety disorders presenting with cravings or restlessness
Cannabis use via vaping devices (refillable pods may aerosolize marijuana oils)
nonInfectiousMimics: Withdrawal-related irritability and restlessness mimicking primary anxiety or depressive disorders
Chronic cough from smoking-related mucous hyperplasia mimicking other causes of chronic productive cough
additionalInvestigations: Structured history of total daily frequency of all nicotine products used (cigarettes, cigars, roll-your-own, vaping, oral pouches/snuff)
Duration of regular use, prior quit experiences, and current interest in quitting
Markers of addiction intensity: episodes per day, spacing through the day, and use within 30 minutes of waking
Biomarkers of smoke-toxicant exposure (markedly lower in exclusive e-cigarette users than in cigarette smokers)
redFlags: Continued smoking during chemotherapy or radiation, associated with poorer outcomes and reduced survival
Smoking in pregnancy: premature rupture of membranes, abruptio placentae, placenta previa, preterm delivery, small-for-gestational-age, increased perinatal mortality and sudden infant death syndrome
Dual use of e-cigarettes and combusted cigarettes, which negates toxicant-reduction benefits
High-frequency use of noncombusted inhaled nicotine products in patients who never used combusted tobacco
Multiplicative cardiac risk when smoking is combined with hypertension or elevated lipids
Higher vascular graft occlusion rates in smokers after bypass surgery
harrison.prognosis: Cessation produces substantial reversible benefit: risk of a second coronary event falls within 6-12 months, and first myocardial infarction and coronary death rates decline within 2-4 years; after about 15 years of abstinence cardiovascular risk approaches that of never-smokers. Cancer risk declines relative to continued smoking after about 4 years, but a roughly three- to fourfold excess lung cancer risk persists even 20 years after quitting. Small-airway changes in young smokers reverse after 1-2 years of abstinence; in established airflow obstruction cessation mainly slows further decline rather than restoring lung function. Quitting is typically cyclical with multiple attempts: about 70-80% of smokers want to quit and over half try in a given year, but only about 6% remain abstinent at 6 months and about 3% at 2 years; systemwide tracking and assistance can raise 12-month abstinence to as high as 25%.
pitfalls: Assuming cigars or pipe tobacco are lower-risk: most cigars are now made like cigarettes and most pipe tobacco is used for roll-your-own, so risks are similar; clinicians should ask about and not recommend them.
Treating 'low tar/nicotine' cigarettes as safer; compensatory smoking negates any benefit and design changes have raised adenocarcinoma rates.
Focusing only on cigarettes and missing cumulative nicotine intake from vaping, oral pouches, and other products when assessing addiction intensity.
Overlooking smoking-induced cytochrome P450 changes when adjusting drug doses around hospitalization or discharge.
Dismissing patients not currently interested in quitting; many still attempt cessation in the subsequent year and benefit from a clear personalized message.
Equating exclusive e-cigarette use (lower toxicant exposure) with cessation of addiction, since persistent nicotine dependence and relapse risk remain.
harrison.severityClassification: No formal grading is presented; addiction intensity is gauged clinically by cumulative daily dosing frequency across all products, spacing of use through the day, use within 30 minutes of waking, craving during abstinence, and history of failed quit attempts.
management: Offer behavioural support and structured cessation counselling as the foundation of every quit attempt
Provide first-line pharmacotherapy with nicotine replacement therapy, varenicline or bupropion to blunt withdrawal and craving
Combine a long-acting nicotine patch with a short-acting form (gum, lozenge, spray or inhalator) for heavier dependence to match self-titrated dosing
Anticipate and support the patient through withdrawal, which intensifies over the first weeks of abstinence, and provide relapse-prevention strategies with scheduled follow-up
Address comorbid mental illness and other substance use that undermine cessation
In pregnancy prioritise behavioural support, using nicotine replacement therapy where needed given the pregnancy risks of continued nicotine
Consider switching to lower-toxicant delivery as harm reduction when abstinence cannot be achieved, since most disease burden comes from the toxicants carried with nicotine
